utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, it's you again. Who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Still Lieutenant-Colonel Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of course. We didn't complete him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to come in I want to introduce a new face at our table today. This is Mr. Colin Nawrot, he will be assisting Mr. Reid and perhaps filling in for him in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Cepic will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave yesterday continues to apply to your evidence until it's complete. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Have you had a rest?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's good then. I'll take up where I left off yesterday you explained to us the use of various frequencies, could you tell me about the chains of command, how did that function.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it functioned in the following way, the commander of the combat unit, from my brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let's just make this brief.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the command of the units of the army, the commander of MUP commanded the units of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not quite clear in the transcript. Were the chains of command separate?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have on our screens 5D931, please. [Interpretation] Your Honours, just before we take a look at this exhibit, page 2, please, line 8, or rather, page 2, line 8, once again not a clear answer, so can we listen to the tape or -- so that we can specify what the witness actually said, not to have to repeat the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm in no doubt that this witness has said that there are two separate chains of command for MUP and VJ, and that was his position yesterday evening as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, can you see the document on our screens?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you see this kind of document, or rather, were you aware of the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was at the point in time when it was distributed to us by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, what was the purpose of this and similar documents, similar orders?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this order was that the senior officers of the unit should become more serious or preventive in actual fact. According to our rules and regulations, instructions, and laws, we were otherwise bound in general terms to respect and apply the provisions of international war law, and this was just one, if I can put it this way, preventive order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, did you perhaps -- were you perhaps present in some actions during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain actions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there an example in which these actions came across civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we came across civilians on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember a specific example that you could give us?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have a number of examples that I remember, but the most -- the one that left the greatest impression on me was refugees escaping in the village of Banja, refugee camp near Banja, that is east of Malisevo when along the fringes of the forest, in my rough estimation some thousand people gathered, women and children, of course. And among them, quite openly, members of the KLA moved around amongst them. They were armed and wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me when that was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the beginning of the NATO aggression, that is to say at the end of March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time, did the unit continue to advance?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit did not continue to advance, but it stopped there. It was not provoked by the presence of the KLA because they were mixed up with the population and we -- they reported about what they found, and the order arrived that the unit should go back to its area of deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system 5D946, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, do you recognise this document, whose it is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at the heading, I see that it's a document from my own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have count 5, please, second page in B/C/S, probably in English also.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you explain item 5, please, especially the sentence where it says that the civilians were sent back and that activities have been intensified.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the terrorists jeopardized part of the road running from Pristina to Pec, from Komorane to Lapusnik, so on that side where the villages are mentioned here, that's where an action was executed and they were pushed back to Mount Drenica. And during their withdrawal with them, they took the civilian population from the villages mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What did they need the civilian population for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian population always, at all times whenever we came across a situation like that, they used as protection against us; and they led the population outside villages with them when they had no other protection, means of protection, they took them to the mountains or to the forest because they knew that we wouldn't go into action when the civilians were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course if I might be allowed to add, we wrote here that the civilians went back although we were at the outskirts of those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D949, please, count 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, can you see the heading of this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at item 5 now, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether of this the basic tactics employed by the Siptar terrorist unit, ambush actions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of their tactics, they apply guerilla tactics and put up ambushes and mines and explosive devices along the roads that they expected people to be moving, or rather, the organs of the state to be moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D947, please. 5D947.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, is this a document from your brigade again?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document from my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you take a look at item 3.2, please, the second paragraph there.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What does the M-77 uniform mean? What kind of uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The M-77 uniforms were olive-green uniforms of the type worn by the JNA and the Territorial Defence in earlier years, until the new uniform had been introduced with the M-89 camouflage pattern. And it was also used by the terrorists because they were stray uniforms that had been left over from the Territorial Defence of the day. And we could see that personally in -- during combat and also on pictures that we came across or footage or the material that we found in their base.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, Witness Shukri Gerxhaliu testified before this Chamber and in his testimony, he stressed that in the village of Donja Sudimlje on the 31st of May, people were killed, or rather, nine members of the Gerxhaliu family were killed. Do you know anything about that, Donja Sudimlje and the date is the 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it that. I know that the incident took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what actually happened, what your knowledge of that is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I received information that something had happened, or rather, that there had been a killing in the village of Donje Sudimlje, and I reported to my commander about that and told him that I would investigate what had happened. I went to the investigating judge of the military wartime court of the Pristina Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to object about this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is nothing that was noticed in the 65 ter summary for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we said we'd describe the work of the security organs, and this is an example of how they worked, how they functioned, and what they did, their concrete activities. He's not a troop officer. He deals with security, and we did inform the other side what the remit and competencies of the security organs were, what they actually did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's impossible for the Prosecution to be prepared for this if you haven't indicated the date or place of the event that you're going to be leading evidence on. Since you haven't intimated it, move on to something else, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, did you have a military police company within your composition?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the war I did have a military police company of a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the basic task of the military police company?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic task of the military police company was to provide security for the command post and rear command post, to provide security for the commander while stationary and while on the move, and the encryption station as well, protection and security for the encryption station, so that would be basically what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me now --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain to me, Lieutenant-Colonel, how the areas of deployment of the units were secured?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, that the command post was secured by the military police units or my company of the military police unit, the units secured -- had their own security for their area of deployment. They would set up guards and reporting stations, and that's how they provided combat security.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D1288, please, 5D.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, Colonel, this is a document from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have count 12, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to this document I have one objection. In the English translation at the bottom of line 6 it says there's a line missing, and it appears that's because in the B/C/S the copy that we have is cut off. I don't know what it says, but it talks about: "Eliminate the shortcomings and take concrete measures aimed at ..." And that's what's missing. That could be something significant for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's paragraph 6 in the English. You will see right before number 7 it says "line missing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're on the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you look at the B/C/S, it's at the very bottom of page 1 it appears that when this Xerox copy was made, it didn't catch the last line because item number 7 starts at the top of the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should endeavour with the witness to complete paragraph 6 if you can, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will try to do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, will you please have a look at paragraph 6. This is not what I was meaning to ask you about, but just to dispel any doubts. Can you explain what this is in relation to, this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is about security and stepping up combat-readiness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help us by telling us what's missing from the end of paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can assume, based on the overall context, the chiefs of combat arms will be engaged as needed and as planned as subordinated units to give expert assistance, eliminate the shortcomings and take concrete measures aimed at strengthening, stepping up combat-readiness, I assume that's what's missing because that's what the whole document is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have second page in B/C/S and count 12, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, do you see item 12, it's right in front of you. Is this your explanation in relation to the security regime in the deployment area? Is your explanation confirmed by this item?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what this item is addressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. Will you please now explain about outside the deployment area, the spaces in between, as it were, were you in charge of controlling those areas?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Outside the deployment areas there were other state bodies that were responsible, the MUP, civil defence, and civil protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if your unit had any check-points?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my unit had none.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And do you perhaps know, given your position, what the jurisdiction was over so-called mixed check-points?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the area of deployment of my unit, there was such a mixed check-point on the way into Pristina from the direction of Kosovo Polje, but it wasn't manned by my unit but rather by the 52nd Military Police Battalion and a component of the MUP who were there at the check-point. The responsibility of the military policemen who were manning the check-point was to inspect incoming military traffic and military personnel passing through. When I say "military personnel," I mean officers, ordinary soldiers, and any other corps members.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about anyone else apart from the military, were the military policemen there in charge of inspecting those persons too?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, did you have a team in your brigade that was in charge of clearing the terrain, sanitization?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was a sanitization team as we called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 5D937.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, is this a document produced by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we're waiting for page 2 to come up, will you tell me if perhaps you know who was in charge of the sanitization, which body?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same unit that was in charge of overall combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. We have a table there of sanitization as carried out. What are these abbreviations about, VJ MUP CZ?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in charge of sanitization, VJ Ministry of the Interior or civil protection. As we can tell based on the face of this document, it was civil protection and the people who were carrying out the sanitization in this particular area of this responsibility at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do we see that on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the table right in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the "Carried out by ..." heading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about sanitization in terms of animal remains and other types of toxic waste on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 5D934, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, you see the document in front of you. Was the document produced by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have count 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Cepic please be asked to speak up a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Does this item confirm what you just said?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise to interpreters and I will follow your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see the second half of item 3, military and judicial organs are invited to launch possible investigations. All right, in a nutshell you explained that already so now we're free to move on to something else. Lieutenant-Colonel, another topic, volunteers, did your unit take in any volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the war some were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was their status after being received into the unit?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same status as all the other soldiers who were in that unit, they were volunteers in terms of the way they joined; but once they were part of the unit they were just ordinary soldiers like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D936, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, is this a document produced by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you encountered any situations where you had to turn away certain persons who volunteered to join the unit?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of situations like that. They were first screened and vetted at recruitment centres, and then they would go to someone to express their desire to set up their own unit, a volunteers' unit as it were. We made no allowances for that. Our personnel sector would send them on an individual basis to other units in the brigade. I once had occasion to turn some of them away and send them back where they came from, in this case the recruitment centre in Belgrade because they refused to be that type of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was a military territorial detachment resubordinated to the brigade at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know when exactly resubordinated from the beginning of the war, the 54th Military Territorial Detachment, yes, they were, Vucitrn.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Where were they deployed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brigade is an armoured brigade. We were always short of infantry, so they were deployed together with a battalion from the 15th Armoured Brigade in the general Vucitrn area, both to the north and to the south of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were they securing a facility or a building in the town of Vucitrn itself?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they weren't in Vucitrn itself, they were deployed around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, did the brigade suffer any losses?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both in 1998 and in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How many people came to grief, officers and ordinary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 there were seven of us and in 1999, 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What were most of the losses caused by?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the losses were caused by terrorist activity in the way that I've already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, were any perpetrators of crimes prosecuted in your unit, were there any crimes to begin with?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you track down those people and did you prosecute them, did you press charges?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time we found that a crime had occurred, we pressed charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about those crimes that are normally deemed most serious, for example, violations of humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were none of those as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What sort of crime was prosecuted? What was the type of crime that you normally came across?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part crimes against property, aggravated theft, theft, motor vehicles that were seized, and typical military violations such as desertion, violations of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a couple of names, by names I mean people you prosecuted for theft for seizing vehicles belonging to other persons, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This all happened quite a long time ago. I'll do my best to remember a couple of names for you. There was an NCO sergeant first class Fuad Musinovic, I think, warrant officer Stevan Radic, warrant officer Kordic; I can't remember his first name. I don't think I can remember anyone else but there is a list of persons who were prosecuted for these crimes, it's in the archives of the military court. I'm not sure in which file you can find members of my brigade, but it should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in General Gojovic's lists, and those are marked P954, some of those names are under number 4, then also under number 30; and in P955, aggravated theft, 146 and 147, two officers from the 15th Brigade are listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, do you know General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How long have you known him for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1993. At that time he became my commander at the communications regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about General Lazarevic as a person and an officer?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that he was and still is a model, my personal model to which I aspire in terms of military career and human qualities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you spent the entire period of war in the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the sons of General Lazarevic, whether they were members of the army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that the oldest and middle son were members of the army, and I know both of them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What status did the two of them have?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, they had the status of soldiers, troops in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did they have any sort of privileges? Were they privileged in any way?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was my last and final --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment before you sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we've had a chance to look at the prior evidence in relation to the incident involving the Gerxhaliu familiar that was referred to. It is part of the Prosecution case. I don't think it would really be in the interests of justice to maintain that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's the precise nature of my objection, though, Your Honour. If it's to confront a Prosecution witness and an incident presented by the Prosecution, that's the very most important kind of thing we should receive note of because when I give lists what I'm going to use in my cross-examination, if I don't know he's going to talk about that incident I don't look at documents relating to that or that prior witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So at the very least, Your Honour, I would need more time to address that if you're going to allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that entirely, on the other hand it's one of these matters that is likely to arise at some stage in a Defence case, and therefore the basic point of notice in principle doesn't arise. It's just a practical technical issue which we recognise and obviously if a remedy is necessary and if the witness has to come back, then we would accommodate that in the circumstances. But, Mr. Cepic, I think I was precipitate in preventing you from dealing with that issue, but you should bear in mind that where the Prosecution had led evidence about a specific event and you have a witness who's going to deal with that event and it's not immediately obvious that he will be dealing with it, then specific notice ought to be given to the Prosecution that that will arise in the course of the evidence. But on this occasion we will re-consider the decision we made earlier and allow you to go into that issue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to refer you to an example in practice, how we were notified by the Prosecution concerning the testimony of witnesses K-54 and K-82; later on it turned out that they were going to testify about some matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, I mentioned earlier and now I would like you to explain to us the following: Prosecution witness Shukri Gerxhaliu in his statement testified about an incident which happened on the 31st of May, 1999, in a village called Donje Sudimlje. Will you please tell us what you personally know, what you personally experienced about what happened there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to the point where I was saying that I informed my commander about what I knew, and then I went to an investigative judge of the military court within our corps and reported what I knew. He ordered that an investigation be launched. We established a team comprising two military policemen. My clerk, myself, and a crime technician from the 52nd Battalion of the military police as well as crime technician from the Vucitrn internal affairs department. I think it was internal affairs department. We went to Donje Sudimlje and we came to the house of the Gerxhaliu family, outside of that house. There were residents, local residents in the village. The investigative judge was conducting his work, collecting information from the residents who appeared there on the spot and who spoke Serbian. I, for my part, talked to two women in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you enter the house?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The judge ordered us to enter the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you come across any traces there, corpses?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not come across any corpses, and we had had some information that we gathered when talking to these people and when collecting information, the people that we met outside of the gate, that's what I mean. As for the traces, there were many of them in the house as well as outside the house. There was coagulated blood in the courtyard and there were traces of murder, traces indicated that there had been a murder committed in the house. The traces consisted of bloody spots on the walls, on bed linen, and we also found traces of bullets that had been fired, casings. The most numerous ones were of 7.62-millimetre calibre, Chinese manufacture with grey casings, and there were several holes on the walls produced by bullets. The people whom we had found in the village explained to us that the corpses had been buried in the village graveyard, that the residents buried them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The investigative team, did they proceed to the graveyard later on?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to the investigative judge, as I have spoken to the women previously, I told the judge that the women told me that in the upper part of the village we could come across the members of the KLA and that it wasn't safe to proceed further on. Since the judge was in charge of the investigation, I told him about this information and I asked him whether he wanted us to move on, to go further, and he ordered us to move towards the graveyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was there an incident on your way to the graveyard?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the team set out, after some 200 metres very intense fire was opened in our direction from this school which was a large building in that village. They opened fire from infantry weapons and machine-guns. Since the Pinzgauer vehicle from my military police company was heading the column, the vehicle was damaged in the course of that attack and it remained in the village. A crime technician from the internal affairs department in Vucitrn was wounded in the hand. Warrant officer, Jovasevic, crime technician from the 52nd Battalion of the military police lost his pistol as they were withdrawing. In other words, they barely managed to survive that ambush. Then the investigative judge ordered us to return to Pristina, saying that the investigation was completed, on-site investigation was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add, we wanted to come on the following day to retrieve the vehicle that had been damaged; however, when we came there the vehicle was gone and we supposed that the KLA members had taken it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me what date it was when you conducted that on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in early June, I think the 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, thank you very much. Those were my questions.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, why did you think this was a matter for the military to investigate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A part of my unit was located in an area above the village, and we didn't want to leave any stone unturned. We didn't want to leave anything to chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Had there already been a MUP investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. You'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis -- sorry, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will be brief, but I do have some cross for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day Lieutenant-Colonel Marinkovic, my name is Dan Ivetic and I am one of the Defence attorneys for Sreten Lukic. Today I'll have just some brief questions for you and would therefore ask you to pay close attention to my questions, and if they're not clear to you please ask me to repeat them. Now, in your direct examination -- pardon me. In your direct examination you talked about a variety of anti-terrorist actions or combat that you were involved in. Were there anti-terrorist actions undertaken by your brigade or any other VJ units in -- near or surrounding your area of responsibility that were undertaken without the utilisation of MUP forces or without the participation of MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such actions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the 54th Military Territorial Detachment as being subordinated to you or your brigade. Were there other military territorial detachments in or near your zone of deployment or responsibility that were not subordinated to your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other military territorial detachments in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Every military department, as far as I know, had military territorial detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could focus in the zone of responsibility of your brigade in particular, do you know if there were any other military territorial detachments of any nature within that particular confined area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, yes, but they were not resubordinated to my brigade as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how many there were and if you know any of their numerical designations?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how many there were. Well, I can't tell you, perhaps the 115th Territorial Detachment is from Kosovo Polje area, I don't know, either it was 115th or 113th, I know it was a three-digit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if there was the 174th in addition to the 115th Military Territorial Detachment?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. I don't think I have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Lieutenant-Colonel. I wanted to ask you a few questions about your background prior to 1998. I understand you began active service in the VJ in 1990. Can you tell us what your first job or first duty was at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first duty was commander of telephone and teleprinter platoon in the communications regiment, in the Skopje garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from there where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Skopje, I became commander of the 1st Platoon in the radio relay company of the same unit; and then in 1992, I was transferred with my unit to the Nis garrison when Macedonia seceded, separated itself, from the rest of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you first become engaged in security work in the army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1997 I was admitted into the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As what? As an operative?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I became chief of security in the 309th Communications Regiment, chief of security organ, that's the formal title in our army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I had not realized, your active service did not begin until 1990; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, in 1990 I graduated from the military academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hate to tell you what's noted here as your date of birth. I'm just trying to see in the transcript what was said yesterday. Yes, your date of birth was given yesterday as the 23rd of April, 1947. I did at the time think that you were very well-preserved for your year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there's a mistake here in the name of my unit. It's not 309th, but rather 319th Communications Regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you were born in Vrbovo, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, those are not my details.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is -- it's our previous witness I'm again confusing you with. I'm very sorry about that, sorry; and I see now -- if you look at the transcript 20132 -- Ah, yes, I have it now. Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, what work have you been engaged in since 1999 when the war ended? You're still active-duty I take it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You are interested in the time-period after the war, after 1999, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Together with my unit, I was transferred to Prokuplje garrison, where I served at the same position, chief of security organ in the 15th Armoured Brigade, I stayed there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 2000, sometime in June 2000 or July, when I went to the department, security department of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there until January 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And between January 2001 and today?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between January 2001 and today, I worked for a year in an expert team of the General Staff for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, and afterwards in the administration for security of the General Staff of the army in Belgrade. And afterwards, I went for additional training to the command staff school for two years, and now I'm a teacher at the school centre for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, is that the body that you talked about for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, is that the Commission For Cooperation that was established by General Pavkovic when he was Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who established it or who had the right, to be quite frank, to set it up; but there was an establishment book appointing me to that particular work post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know how you got appointed to that post, did someone contact you in advance and interview you or tell you you were being considered? How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As every time, whenever I was reassigned, I received an order saying that I was being reassigned to another post for the requirements of the service in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from whom did this particular order come from, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was a lieutenant-colonel by rank. Now, I can't remember which service it was whose job it was to compile that order, but it's all regulated in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if General Lazarevic recommended you for that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When were you promoted to lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the rank of lieutenant-colonel, I think in April 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At the age of 33?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was promoted ahead of time twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the nature of your work as an expert for this commission? What did you do exactly? Did you gather documents? Did you interview people? What were your tasks?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was in the analytical department of that team, my tasks were mostly to do with studying all the documents to see whether they were complete and to distribute those same documents when required by the centre for cooperation. I also took part in preparing the documents in order for them to be sent off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, is getting far away from the subject in hand, and if we're discussing 2001 or 2002 or whatever year after that, I don't think it's going to take us anywhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This -- the subject here is not 2001 or 2002, but how the documents from 1998 and 1999 were treated before they were sent to the Office of the Prosecutor, and indeed there is the other subject of the great difficulty that the Office of the Prosecutor did have in securing a great many of the documents that are relevant in the case. So this is a relevant issue for this trial. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you said that you took part in preparing the documents in order for them to be sent off. What kind of work did -- what kind of work required a lieutenant-colonel to prepare the documents for them to be sent off? That sounds more like a job for a private clerk. What were you doing to prepare these documents?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, the documents that were requested, we would search for them in the archives, find them, copy them, attach a letter to them, and send them on to the centre. A private clerk cannot do that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why not? Why can't a private clerk search the archives and find documents? It's not that complicated, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's probably not that complicated, but I don't think he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there were times when you couldn't find some of the documents requested by The Hague Tribunal, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly, but as I said I was in the analytical department. There were other departments who, in concrete terms, went to look for the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to something else. You were in the security - what's the term I should use? - security administration of the army or is it a department? What's the correct name?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a clerk in the security department, in one of the sectors of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in 19 -- from July 1998 to the end of the war in June 1999, who was your immediate superior? To whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the brigade commander, and in the professional sense the chief of the security sector of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, yeah. Could you explain about that a little bit. We've heard from some other witnesses that in the security sector or the security service, security administration, that you actually report up two chains. One is to the commander of the brigade, but don't you also report separately through the security channels? Isn't that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly as the security organs in the brigade, we were subordinated to the brigade commander. Now, for all questions, and we took part in the work of the brigade command, but for all questions that which to security, the security of the brigade, of the members of the brigade, we would report to the brigade commander about that and the chief of security of the corps. Now, there was certain issues since we had authorisation to apply certain methods, secret methods, then the brigade commander did not know about those things; so about those things and other information we would report to the chief of security in the corps, and that was the rule regulated by the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the chief of security in the corps at the time was who?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security of the corps in 1998 and 1999 was Colonel Momir Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you send him written reports or was it only oral reports or was it both?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how often would you report to him in the last half of 1998 and the first half of 1999? Was it once a day? Once a week?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would report to him twice a day, and if there were any events that had taken place then more than that, depending on urgency, on a need-to-know basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where in the VJ archives would your reports, those kind of reports, be kept?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that all my operative documents, as a rule at the beginning of the war, I would destroy and take with me only the mobilisation documents. Now, where the documents from the sector are, I don't know, and what way they were dealt with I really can't say. I think they were duty-bound to destroy their documents too at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about documents generated during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents generated during the war -- well, I didn't find them in the corps when I took over my post in 2000. Quite possibly they exist somewhere in the archives in Belgrade, but I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't have occasion to look for them or come across them when you were working as an expert for the Commission For Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, and I've told you that I did not deal with that. I told you what the team dealt with in principle. I was in the analytical department and the documents arrived in my department and then we forwarded them on to the centre, as I explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I didn't understand in that explanation was what you do in the analytical department, once you had made it clear you don't search for the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As there were a number of departments, our department was the department where the collected documents arrived pursuant to a request from this Tribunal, or rather, the centre who sent the request on to us. So we would look at the numbers, compare them, whether they were the right documents and right attachment letters, and then send them off to the centre for cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 when you were working in security in the 15th Armoured Brigade, how many people worked directly for you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, establishment-wise my clerk and myself, but as the situation became more complex in Kosovo we would be helped out from the security organs of the army who sent us their operatives in order to strengthen the combat groups and not to leave anything to chance so that we were better informed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At most, what was the highest number then of people you had working for you in, let's say, 1999 when additional operatives were sent to help with the combat groups?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's differentiate between two periods, one is in 1999 before the war when the operatives were sent to help out, and in each of the three or four combat groups, depending on the situation when they were formed; and in 1999 again, I was replenished with my own establishment security organs from the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you give us the two numbers for those different periods?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the first period there were up to six of us, and during the war, let me just remember, there were eight of us. I think there were eight of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of work did these operatives do then? Are they wearing military uniform or are they wearing civilian clothes and going out and gathering intelligence? What did they do in general terms?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all in uniforms during the war, and we had our operative positions in the units. We would gather all the information that had to do with jeopardizing security in the units, whether from the unit or from outside towards the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about in --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't mean to cut you off if you had something more to say on that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about in the first part of 1999 before the war started, did they all wear uniforms then or did they do their work in civilian clothes sometimes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They mostly wore uniforms, and my clerk and myself would wear civilian clothes from time to time as well because of the nature of the business.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the nature of the business is such that sometimes you're going out and talking to civilians and you want to be wearing civilian clothes, not to be recognised as being in the army, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes there was the need to talk to civilians too in order to gather information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your civilian sources that you got information from, did you pay them or did they just volunteer information? What was the nature of that relationship in your intelligence gathering?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never paid a single civilian for any intelligence. Quite simply, there were people who had enough consciousness security-wise, saw that there were problems, and wanted to help and convey that to the state organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's the nature of that kind of work, isn't it, that sometimes you are given misinformation or disinformation by persons who have interests contrary to your own, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there were quite a lot of people who wanted to plant disinformation on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about a couple of the exhibits that Mr. Cepic showed you or that were on the list to be used with you. One of them you mentioned the incident where you -- you and your driver were attacked on the road I think between Podujevo and Pristina when your car was shot up. Do you recall that one?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I recall it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It said in that report that you were in a civilian vehicle with civilian tags and you were wearing civilian clothes, that you had come back from a meeting of something that is listed as the OUP is the English acronym. Can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Department of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that meeting to share intelligence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The purpose of that meeting was to exchange information about the territory and that was one of four meetings that I had in the space of the four days pursuant to an order from my superior, the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You worked in communications. I think you told us -- it was translated in English as a signalsman. Is there any substantive difference or distinction between that term "signalsman" or "communications officer"? Are those basically the same thing or is there some distinction?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean liaison officers which were established when the OSCE mission came and officers in the signals part of the army, then there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't talking about the liaison with the OSCE. Maybe it's just we use the same terms somewhat interchangeably in English. I take it then that you mean -- you worked in communications, for example, radio communications, telegraphic communications, all manner of communications, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was the officer there, communications officer in the military specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's common practice, isn't it, Lieutenant-Colonel, for in the military to use code-names or call-signs to identify various units or organs for purposes of, to some extent, protecting the identity of a unit when you're communicating, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army, yes, there is this communication practice which has the highest level of military secret where that exists and where they are listed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall in 1998 and/or 1999 what code-name or call-signs were connected with the 15th Armoured Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The call-sign in communications is composed of two parts. One part is the name and the second part is the identification number of the officer, or rather, the person who is going to respond when you call him up using that call-sign. So, for example, in the brigade, the brigade I was in the identification number was Grom, and my number was 242. So for somebody to respond when you call him up with the call-sign, you have to say Grom, G-r-o-m, and 242, and I would come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the commander of the brigade was Colonel Cirkovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, the -- Colonel Cirkovic, Mladen Cirkovic was the head of the 15th Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what his call-sign was in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might be wrong, but it was Grom 215. I'm not sure about that number, whether it was 215 that was his number, but it was changed from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the unit, the 15th or subordinate units of the 15th Armoured Brigade, using code-name or call-sign Goles, G-o-l-e-s with the full banana?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible as far as 1998 goes, but I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what name was used by the Pristina Corps in either 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name that was used during one period was Pastrik. It was changed in 1998 and 1999, but I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P1052.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, there are three pages of a document that's called: "Communications station work-plan." If you could look at the first page here. There's no reference to the 15th -- I'm sorry, let me see which one we've got up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The B/C/S doesn't match the English page we've got on the screen so if we could go one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, have you seen these kind of work-plans before?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forms like this of a work-plan is a military work-plan and in the upper left-hand corner it says "form DV-6," so that's the communications form. This is the standard type of form used, and I've seen many similar ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the third page of both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a couple more questions for you before the break. Lieutenant-Colonel, at the top you'll see a reference to a body called the Joint Command with the call signal, call-sign, of Pastrik. And right below that you see the forward command post for the Pristina Corps having call-sign of Pastrik 13. Do you recall seeing or hearing or using either of those call-signs during either 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to mention first of all that this document was not properly filled out from the professional point of view as a communications officer, I noticed that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel. Could you just answer my question first.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see this document. I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was: Do you recall seeing or hearing or using those call-signs, Pastrik, in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pastrik 13, that was the one we used. Pastrik is incorrect, Pastrik as it is, just that single word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And number 8 -- I'm sorry. I don't have -- number 7 -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could I go to another English page -- perhaps, Your Honour, this is the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, we have to have a break at this stage; while we have it, would you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, one last thing with regard to those communications plans. I wanted to look at the one that is B/C/S page number, the last four digits are 3242, I think it's the second page among the B/C/S. There's a reference to what appears to be the 3rd Battle Group of the 15th Armoured Brigade and the 2nd Battle Group of the 15th. Do you see that --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there's a reference to call-signs or call signals of Goles 80 and Goles 70. Do you recall those call-signs being used by subordinate units of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are code-names for units from the communications plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to show you Exhibit 3D1004, 1004. This is from the 21st of August, 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the Trial Chamber has taken a clear-cut position on newspaper articles. I don't think that any sort of cross-examination at all can be based on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know that is not our position. The position we take depends obviously on the potential relevance of answers to the questions formulated by reference to newspaper reports, so let's hear what the question is first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my question is, Your Honour, I'm not sure that that's the document I'm looking for. I have 3D1004, 1004, as being a 21st of August, 1998, Pristina Corps command security section report. And what I printed out yesterday and had a hard copy, that's the number I took it from in e-court, 3D1004. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You now have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General [sic], it's page 1 for you. Have you seen these kind of documents before in your work?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen this sort of document. It's a security section telegram. I used to work for them at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this one is from the 21st of August, 1998, and it's -- the name at the bottom is Colonel Djindjic. Did you know Colonel Slobodan Djindjic in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did he work for then?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was with the security department in the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What was his position vis-a-vis Colonel Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a representative of the superior security organ, but he was not his superior officer. That was Colonel Petar Kuzmanovic at that time as far as I remember, the chief of security department of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1998 you were aware, were you not, of the existence of a body that was called the Joint Command that met regularly in Pristina in July through October of 1998? Did you know about them back then?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't know about them in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you look at item number 3 in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have to go to page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see it makes reference to: "From the operative report of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija we would like to mention the following ..." Does not suggest to you, sir, that there was some body called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in August 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of principle, when I read this I see that it says "report by the Joint Command." This was something that was forwarded by the State Security Service, but as a matter of fact at the time I was not aware of any such body or knew of any such body. I knew of the corps command that was my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit P2945.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This pertains to Colonel Stojanovic. This is a newspaper article purporting to record an interview with him. Were you aware of that or did you ever see that article --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has not been announced. It's not on the document list of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I thought I had it on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's ask the question without the document, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wanted to show him the report on page 2, which is a report from Colonel Stojanovic to the Joint Command on the 10th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is -- it's a copy of that order, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or report rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We saw it before. It's item number 2 on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It should have been notified, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Is there any explanation for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, apparently that's just human error on this human's part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, it would assist us, I think, to hear what the witness can say on this, and it is a document which has featured in the trial in the course of this week. It doesn't seem to us that there could be any real prejudice caused to you in the circumstances, and therefore we'll excuse the failure and allow these questions to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the English I think we need to have page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, can you make that out on the screen in front of you? I know it may not be very legible, but it's entitled --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite illegible. Perhaps if you point me to the precise spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the title --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the top of the page it has: "Pristina Corps command, security sector, 11 November 1998." And it says: "To the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this was provided in a newspaper interview that Colonel Stojanovic gave when he was talking about events in 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo, and it too tends to show the existence of a body called the Joint Command. That doesn't refresh your memory about whether such a body existed and the security organ, security sector, were aware of it and actually reporting to it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of it at the time, no. As far as I can tell, this is a document produced by the security section. I had no authority to inspect any documents within the possession of my superior officer, and I've certainly never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when was the first time that you heard of such a body as the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija? You must have heard about it before you came here yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had heard of it while following the trial here in The Hague, and I also heard of it as I was being proofed by my lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't hear of it back when you were working as an expert for the VJ commission for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal? Documents weren't requested regarding the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have heard, but I don't remember. I'm only telling you what I'm sure I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at whatever point in time when you may have first heard of it, you weren't motivated to ask General Lazarevic or General Pavkovic or Colonel Stojanovic about what the Joint Command was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't motivated. I know what the command system worked like in the corps, therefore I definitely had no need to ask questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you know what it worked at -- worked like at your level, at the 15th Brigade, correct, but you don't know what it worked like at the higher levels, do you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew how the corps command was exercising command over the 15th Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't know about the Joint Command meetings that General Lazarevic attended in 1998, do you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't know about the dozens of Joint Command meetings that General Pavkovic attended in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you don't know about the October 29th meeting of the inter-departmental staff with President Milosevic, President Milutinovic, General Perisic, General Samardzic, General Pavkovic, General Lukic, and several other high military and political figures in which the Joint Command's accomplishments during the summer of 1998 were discussed in some detail, you don't know about that either, do you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You must be aware of the fact that that was too high level for me at the time. I was captain first class at the time in the position that I was holding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, did you see any document that made reference to the Joint Command, for example, the one that you've mentioned a moment ago that contained information from the state security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've explained, this is a document from the security section, my superior section, the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I misunderstood what you said, and I'll check. Your answer was: "This was something that was forwarded by the State Security Service." Is that a wrong translation of what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not wrong, that's what the sentence says, that it was received from the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The 15th Armoured Brigade's area of responsibility covered what municipalities or parts of municipalities in 1999? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the following municipalities, or rather, parts of municipalities: Pristina municipality, Vucitrn, Kosovo Polje, Lipljan perhaps, parts of Lipljan, and parts of Glogovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your work in 1998 and 1999 I think you told us that you -- you met or coordinated with a counterpart from the State Security Service from the MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
