utterances.text: Yes. I said that in 1998 in addition to my regular duties with the command of the 52nd ARBR PVO. I also offered assistance to the corps's forward command post, so to speak, and then my chief appointed me coordinator with the State Security Service, with the state security branch sector in the Djakovica garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was that individual?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Camovic. I think his first name was Sreten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about in 1999, did you have any regular contact with members of state security?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999 I was in the Pristina garrison. My superior command was based there and they were in charge of this communication with the State Security Service. All I had was what happened through the superior security section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were you physically located most of the time in March through June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent most of that period transferred to the village of Uglari, if I may put it that way. That's just across the way from Kosovo Polje in a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what municipality is that in?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo Polje, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how far from Pristina is that located?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the entry into town itself, the distance may be 2 or 3 kilometres. I never really thought much about that, but there are some industrial facilities along the road, so it's almost the same thing altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look at Exhibit P1996. I'll show you the cover page first and then I'll take you to the page where I have a specific question --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness can hardly be expected to offer relevant information on a document or a meeting that he has never seen and that he did not attend, especially not if we're looking at an entirely different body. This is a document, these are minutes from a MUP meeting. So much for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to point him to the comments by the chief for Pristina, where he's making comments about cooperation with the VJ, problems with VJ soldiers and their conduct, and ask him if that's something he was aware of or whether it's consistent with what he knew about, et cetera. I think that's the kind of thing we've done on a regular basis, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. This last sentence about doing that on a regular basis, my own client, General Lazarevic, was actually disallowed from commenting on this very document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have a reference for that, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my case manager is working on that. I hope we can get it over the next two or three minutes, the exact page of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't need to show him the document, Your Honour, I can just ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but because you insist on doing it we run into these difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think there's anything improper in proceeding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may be right, but I'd like to see what we did on the occasion referred to if you want to insist on using the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'd like to save time and just ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, are you aware that the police in Pristina --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm a lieutenant-colonel by rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, by the way, we still want that reference as soon as you can get it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I promoted you. Sir, the -- are you aware that in May of 1999 the police in Pristina viewed cooperation with the VJ as being poor and claimed that on one occasion Colonel Cirkovic was asked to provide men for a joint and mixed check-point and the VJ soldiers did not show up. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first portion about this being correct or not, I really don't know, but I really don't know if Colonel Cirkovic was ever asked to do anything by the MUP. You know, the corps command can actually order us to set up a check-point, and the MUP can only file this request through the corps command. I don't really know. We didn't have the manpower or the equipment for that. I had reserve military policemen with me and they were securing the check-point. I've told you about this already, haven't I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know about VJ members not stopping at check-points and driving away from the police when they were asked to stop? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one from my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how can you possibly know that? You couldn't have been with every member of your brigade at every check-point they ever went by. You can't possibly know that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of anyone from my brigade doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my hard-working assistant has just located the references, 18807 and -- through 18809, those are the transcript references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The date?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 22nd of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was just checking that to see how that transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were volunteer units in VJ uniforms in Pristina in May -- early May 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the following: During the briefings with the chief of the security section of the corps, and those briefings were held at least once a week or more frequently, even I was given tasks to verify some information. There was some unverified data circulating that there were paramilitary formations, and I personally didn't know about this nor do I know that somebody else was informed that there had been paramilitary formations. And at the time, we had some people who, for reasons only known to them, were misinforming us. So we needed to verify and double verify everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of your duties in the security service to gather intelligence and identify and arrest any perpetrators of crimes, did you come across allegations that MUP members, particularly at the mixed check-points were allegedly engaged in committing crimes against the civilian population, including murder, rape, looting, and robbery? Did you know about that or hear about any of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information concerning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of a report that General Lazarevic wrote on the 24th of May, 1999, speaking specifically about that problem? Did you ever see that or hear that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, was this document sent to my brigade command? If it was, then I probably did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The only copy I have shows it going up --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I think it would be of assistance, if we are referring to the document, to show it to the witness as well so that he knows what he's talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my question was if he was aware that it had been reported. I can show him the document but I'm trying to save time. It's exhibit P1723.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I can hand you a hard copy, Colonel -- Lieutenant-Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While that's happening, now that I've had a chance to see the point in the transcript where Mr. Lazarevic was asked about P1996, the circumstances were completely different from those that we've just faced. It was re-examination on a matter which had already been dealt with and adequately explained by him. What we're dealing with here is cross-examination, quite different situation, and therefore one in which it would have been perfectly proper for Mr. Hannis to make use of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I think it's the sixth paragraph down. Do you see one that talks about the work of mixed check-points? I think it's highlighted in orange on your copy. Yeah. Could you read that one to yourself quickly and then tell us if as of 24th May 1999 you were aware of any allegations like that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of my brigade there was just one mixed check-point, if I remember well. It was at the entry point into Pristina from the direction of Kosovo Polje. This document right now I have never seen before, and I do not have nor did I ever have the information stated here. I never came across such information and my operative work or in my area for which I was responsible as chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you didn't file any reports orally or written to your commander or up to Colonel Stojanovic about that kind of thing, about MUP committing crimes against the civilian population, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the crimes that I learned of, I acted accordingly. If it was committed by a member of the army, then I took measures; and if it wasn't a member of the army who committed them, then I reported further on to my superior. As for matters of these nature, I never informed about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- there are two separate issues in there. There's the issue of problems at mixed check-point, and there's the issue of reporting of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my issue was the reporting of these particular crimes by MUP against civilians, and I take his answer at the end where he says: "As for matters of these nature, I never informed about them." So I take it that means he did not report it up to General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, isn't that right, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no way I could have informed General Lazarevic personally. I was not in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not understanding this, Mr. Hannis. The thing he says he didn't report was problems with the mixed check-points, but your other question was whether he had reported murder, rape, looting, robbery, matters of that nature, and he appears to say that that was reported to his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not clear on that I guess I need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm certainly not clear on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, did you or did you not advise your superiors?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I gave an answer of a general nature, that I always reported on any crimes that I came across. I didn't refer specifically to the crimes mentioned here. Had I come across, and I didn't, had I come across such crimes, I would have reported them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well what --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- We understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What kind of crimes did you come across then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I came across people who had committed looting, confiscated motor vehicles, and I filed criminal complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But they're listed in this paragraph I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but, Mr. President, what is stated here is that given that MUP tolerates crimes committed by their members - and I didn't come across any MUP members who had committed them - I took action with regard to my own people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go next to Exhibit 3D633.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, with the help of the usher I'll trade you documents. This is a -- what's been referred to as an evening briefing session of the Supreme Command Staff on the 2nd of June, 1999. You'll go down to number 3, it's General Farkas --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- These minutes or at least several levels below from the position held by the witness at the time, so I don't see how he can give reliable and relevant information concerning something that was briefed about at the highest level. I'm not quite familiar with the hierarchy, but I'm sure that this is at least five levels above his level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The whole purpose of having a system of course is for information to be relayed up and down, and in cross-examination it's perfectly proper to place before the witness the foundation for the questions. Indeed, the objection's often taken that there's no foundation or the foundation hasn't been adequately set. There's nothing improper in the approach now being taken. If the question asked is objectionable in some way, then we'll deal with that. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you'll see I think the sixth bullet point down under General Farkas. It says: "Crimes are being committed by our units in Kosovo. Reports on these acts are not going through regular channels and lines of command. Are serious things happening that the global public is aware of?" Isn't it true that the crimes that were being committed on the ground weren't being fully reported up through the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two parts to your question. First of all, is it true that there were any crimes? Yes, it is true, and we did our best to prosecute everything that we learned about. I at the position which I held did not receive information that my commander knew about something but did not report on it unless he concealed something from me, which I do not believe is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you'll go down three more bullet points you'll see the entry, it says: "15 bodies were found, including women and children, in the area of the 15th Armoured Brigade." That's your brigade. Were you aware of what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is my brigade, and based on the date when this took place all I can say that it was Donje Sudimlje. I can't remember that there was anything else at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, when you told us about Donje Sudimlje before, did you mention that there were women and children?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that the entire family was involved. That's the information we received. However, we did not complete our investigation on site because of the KLA attack, but based on the information we collected in the village itself we knew that the entire family was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand that from your early testimony. Did you tell us before that you actually found bodies? Wasn't what you told us before that the bodies had been buried in the graveyard and you went to try and locate them when you were fired upon, so you didn't find any bodies, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was clear in my evidence, that there were no corpses there. We came across traces of the crime, signs of the crime, but when upon receiving, collecting, information from the residents we wanted to go to the graveyard, we were preventing brutally from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So from the signs you found at the scene you were able to determine that there were 15 bodies, including women and children, from the blood spatters on the wall and the empty casings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we could not conclude anything about the figure. We could only conclude something about the figure based on the conversations with those who were present. And as I said, we were unable to verify that at the graveyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what did you report up your chain of command about what you found when you went out there on I think you told us it was the -- what day did you say it was, I think you said it was the 5th of June?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This report is the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the report dated the 2nd of June. Based on the information we received, the crime was committed on the 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you first find out about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time, but I can't be more precise than that. I can't remember exactly, but it was during that period of time that we took action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you make a written report about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. So how can you be sure that this isn't referring to some other incident?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that I was sure. I said that based on the date I thought that it was this incident; however, I didn't know that there were any other such cases in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you seen the indictment in this case?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read it carefully, but I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the next bullet point says: "We have problems with the personnel over the appointment of certain senior officers from the security service." Do you know what that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the other side, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what this pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. That's all I had about that one. Do you know who Colonel Stojanovic's counterpart was in the SDB? Who did he liaison with from the Ministry of the Interior in 1998/1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite familiar with the organization of the Ministry of the Interior in order to be able to say anything authoritatively on it, but he most likely stayed in touch with the chief of the sector of the state security in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know a David Gajic in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for this next series of questions, based on what happened the other day with the witness, I think I would request we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What category of person are we concerned about the identification of?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It may affect the safety of at least one individual. I can say more in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In any event, the reason is to ensure the security of an individual who might otherwise be at risk?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that throughout 1998 and 1999 you were sometimes or several times at the command post when anti-terrorist actions were being executed. What were your duties at the command post during such times?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was mostly there as a representative of the command, that is to say I was with my commanding officer there when a subordinate unit would execute actions, whether it was a combat group or a battalion, an establishment unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a representative of the command, what exactly, what precisely, did you do? Were you reading the reports as they came in and analysing the information? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was there in my role as chief of the security organ, and in those units, the ones that were reinforcements to the MUP or launched independent terrorist actions, I had my operative positions and -- or they had their operative positions and I would tell them what to focus on during an action. And it was much easier for me if I was there to understand the situation when I received the reports rather than just receiving reports. So I could see whether something was not according to the regulations or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kinds of things would you task those operatives to do during these actions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they weren't operatives, they were officers and soldiers who voluntarily accepted working on certain affairs and collecting information for the needs of the service. That is why I said operative positions. And I issued tasks to them about anything that could indicate a crime having been committed, that they should focus on that to see whether anything had happened, anything untoward; and if something had, to report to me, whether it ranged from theft to more serious crimes and they would send in their reports to me and report to me at set locations. Of course at the time it was not possible to do that work up at the command post, because the principles of my service is that it maintains secrecy and confidentiality in its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us how you went out and participated in that on-site investigation regarding the Gerxhaliu family on the 5th of June, but earlier in --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- May did you not receive information about the killing of several civilians, the indictment alleges about 104 Kosovo Albanians killed in connection with a large convoy of individuals moving on the Studime gorge road in the direction of the town of Vucitrn. Did you never hear about that incident?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who decided that you would be at this joint or combined command post during these operations? Who told you to go there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brigade commander and I at the collegium, the staff meeting in the morning we would decide who would go to control the subordinate units; it's one of the functions of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Was -- well, what command post are you at then? Are you at a command post of one of the subordinate elements that's engaged in the task? You're not at the overall brigade command post, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood that very well. When the commander appears at a command post, it is the brigade command post at the same time. So in principle, the commander decides where his command post is going to be, and for -- to facilitate the functioning, it's usually at the command post of some lower-down unit when it comes to smaller actions, security is made easier and communications are easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So were you at the same command post that Colonel Cirkovic was at?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you aware of a large convoy of many thousands of people proceeding towards Vucitrn at the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did report to me my operative positions, or rather, my subordinate reserve security organs which I mentioned in my previous testimony that there were certain number of civilians moving at a distance from my unit's combat deployment, so I knew there was a convoy, and I personally saw some convoys along the roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it what you've just said means that your brigade was in a position to observe this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From some elevations, some elevated positions, you would observe that. They were relatively far away from the position where my brigade was deployed, but because of the number of people moving along that way, it was visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that in these actions where there was joint activity with the MUP, that MUP commanders would be present at the command post as well. Do you know any of those MUP commanders that were present at the command post when you were there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can remember -- I could try to remember, but as to names perhaps Zarko Bratkovic -- I really can't remember the names, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned, I think, meeting with your brigade collegium when preparing for these kind of operations or actions. Is that correct? Would there be some sort of planning meeting prior to the activities taking place?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the commander would rally the senior staff, tell us -- give us our tasks that we had got from the corps command to support the MUP forces because you're talking about the joint actions now, that we should reinforce them at such and such an axis for such as a purpose. So he presents his views, he assigns tasks, and that kind of thing, and then we would go on and act upon them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At those meetings, did your commander not show you the order received from the Pristina Corps setting out what the task was for the 15th?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wouldn't show it to us. He would hold a piece of paper like you're holding your document in front of hi, and issue tasks to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you never saw any of these documents that might have "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" at the top?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely didn't see any headings like that during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- did you during some other period?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained when I saw that. Do you want me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean during proofing and preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned in your testimony today at page 13, line 15, about volunteers, and you had once had occasion to turn some of them away and send them back where they came from. When was that that you turned away some volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the beginning of the war, but I can't give you an exact date. Possibly it is to be found in the archives of the documents, but as far as I remember the volunteers were brought in two buses to Kosovo Polje near the command post; and the commander set aside a personnel officer which has the necessary organization and unit formation in order to distribute these volunteers. And as the security organ myself, I was asked to look at their cards to see whether there were any problem people there on the basis of my knowledge, and that was at the beginning of the war sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many did you actually turn away?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now, to give you an exact figure, but no many, about a dozen, ten or so, that did not agree to the conditions we set, that they can't set up a volunteer unit the way they see fit, but they enter the brigade and the general deployment as set.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you mentioned a document. Did you report this then to your brigade commander and/or your security superior?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did inform them. I think I informed them orally, but the personnel organ was duty-bound. I can't say whether they did report, but it was their duty to send on the report to the corps about the reception of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Cepic showed you Exhibit 5D937 which was a report on cleaning up the territory, the burial of certain dead animals. That report was dated the 18th of May and it refers only to dead animals. Did you actually get involved in any sanitation where human beings were buried?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. As you can see on the basis of that document, it was the civilian protection that did that. It wasn't up to my units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we look at 5D946 quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is one that Mr. Cepic showed you as well. This is a report from the 15th Brigade, combat report 25th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need to go to page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I can hand you a hard copy. It's on the second page and it's item number 5 about security. You mention the return of the Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I said, it's dated the 25th of April. When had the Siptar population returned?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That population returned during that period, successively, when the terrorists felt that they didn't need them anymore as a human shield and allowed them to leave, and that's when they returned to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many people are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really give you the number. There were three villages, and I wasn't there in all the places so I really can't say. But if a village has 5 to 600 inhabitants, you can work it out for yourself roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You at page 5 today answered a question about why the KLA needed the civilian population, and you said: "The civilian population always, at all times, whenever we came across a situation like that, they used as protection against us and they led the population outside villages with them when they had no other protection, means of protection. They took them to the mountains or to the forest because they knew that we wouldn't go into action when the civilians were present." Now, this is the 25th of April. You know, sir, don't you, that by the end of the first week in April hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians had already left, some voluntarily, others, we say, by force and gone to Albania and Macedonia. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's rather a long question. I do know that a large number of the Albanian population from Kosovo and Metohija left and went to Albania and Macedonia. Now, what do you want me to answer to the rest of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you say that they always used the civilian population at all times. I say to you that you cannot know that and, as a matter of fact, don't you know that some of the civilians left whenever the army showed up because they knew about incidents in which women, kids, and old people had been killed by Serb security forces. They were afraid of you, that's why they left?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in Donje Sudimlje, I talked to the civilians living in the village and part of my unit was not 500 metres above the village at an elevation and there were inhabitants in the village on the 5th of June so I don't know what you want to say by what you've just stated. What are you implying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm talking about all the other times you said the KLA used civilian as a human shield. I'm saying to you: Isn't it possible that the reason the civilians went on the move when you showed up was because they were afraid of the army, not necessarily because the KLA was using them as a human shield. Do you allow for the possibility that sometimes --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I said. That's right, I said I gave a personal example --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we haven't got the full translation in B/C/S, so could we have it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give the question again, Mr. Hannis, from "isn't it possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Isn't it possible that the reasons the civilians went on the move when you, the VJ, showed up is because they were afraid of the army, not necessarily because the KLA was using them as a human shield. Do you allow for that possibility sometimes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were afraid of the fighting that the KLA provoked on the outskirts of those villages, and they were afraid that they might get hurt in that. And I do claim that the KLA took them with them as a human shield, wherever they couldn't pull out fast enough or didn't have any fortification -- fortified positions or properly fortified positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could I show you Exhibit 5D931. This is a document dated the 30th of March, 1999. You looked at it earlier. And in your answer at page 3, line 7, you said: "The purpose of this order was that the senior officers of the unit should become more serious or preventive in actual fact." Is that because already by the 30th of March there had been problems and it was necessary to issue this kind of instruction or reminder about respecting and applying the provisions of international law?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my brigade, no, and the purpose of this order is and was prevention. As you can see, it was written pursuant to an order from the Pristina Corps command, and then it was sent down the chain to lower units as an order. So have you understood the answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's a matter of semantics, but your answer before was: "The purpose of this order was that the senior officers of the unit should become more serious." To me, in English, that means prior to this date they've been less serious and there's a need to be more serious, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. As a lawyer you look at it that way. Perhaps I used the vernacular when I said "get serious," but the substance of the order is prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness. I did want to note for the record that I have a new face at the table Ms. Wendolijn Kramer, who is part of Mr. Reid's legion of supporters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, your brigade was located in Srbica in late March 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not at any time either at the end of March or the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a few questions, but may I ask them after we take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why? Is it more than five minutes you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I don't know yet. I have to check. I have to check. That is the point, and I have to discuss with my client in -- during the break just to consider what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll have another break at this stage. Again, Mr. Marinkovic, could you please leave the usher. We'll break now and we'll resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, to go back to the question I asked you towards the end of the last session, I'm bringing up on the screen Exhibit P1968, and it's at paragraph 5.3. Now, you'll see in that paragraph a task which was ordered on the 24th of March, 1999, involving villages which are part of the Srbica municipality bordering perhaps on Glogovac and putting your brigade in the area of the south-east perhaps of the -- sorry, south-west of the municipality around the end of March.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an accurate observation. These villages referred to here as the axis of the attack -- perhaps I misunderstood you when you asked me whether I was in Srbica, meaning the village of Srbica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it was my mistake, and it's the municipality I'm concerned about. And the end of the axis referred to there is not very far from the village of -- the populated area of Izbica. Now, we've heard evidence of the killing of a substantial number of people there. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard of that, yes, about the village of Izbica specifically, not at the time, but I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember when you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. I can't be certain. I may have heard during the war at one of the briefings, but I'm certain that I heard about this through the media, the public media, but I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And at the end of March after this order, between then and the end of March, it is your brigade that would be the VJ unit operating in that area, would it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, parts of Glogovac municipality, parts of Kosovo Polje municipality, Vucitrn, Pristina, and parts of Lipljan municipality, the southern parts. Until later on following a defensive operation, we were replaced by other units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Looking at that paragraph, the village of Trdevac is in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Tica do you know where it is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say without a map. I'm really not familiar with the breakdown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Hannis, anything arising from this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, while this is on the screen in front of you, the axis there for the 15th Brigade, how far is that from Izbica, can you determine that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not without a map, I'm sorry. One thing I can say, though, is by looking at these villages they were in the blockade of this sector on the southern slopes of the Kosmet [as interpreted] mountain, I think it's quite far from the mountain, Izbica, and I think our equipment, combat equipment of my brigade couldn't go there, couldn't pass there, it's just the lie of the land that would have made it impossible for us to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In transcript, page 76, line 14, it is not Kosmet, Kosmac mountain and from the mountain Izbica, village Izbica, whatever. Your Honour, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, all my questions stem from Mr. Hannis's questions on the radio system that you were using, the communications system. What was the call-sign for the 15th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the 15th Armoured Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I mean.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at all these documents jogged my memory. I think back in 1998 it was Goles and back in 1999 it was Grom, might have been but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Which one were you using during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was Grom 242 for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have on our screens 5D1052, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this document to come up, Lieutenant-Colonel, back in 1999 during the war were there any combat groups?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, a switch was made to establishment units. So combat groups were disbanded, and then elements of units from various battalions were returned to their own original establishment units. So we were set up as establishment units in defensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 3 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, if you look at this document, do you see any reference there to particular time-frame?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain to the Prosecutor that the document was drawn up in a very poor way, it's inaccurate. You can't tell the time-frame, you can't tell the communications plan that this is based on, and you can't see the level of confidentiality involved. It simply doesn't offer up sufficient elements [as interpreted] for us to analyse anything. I'm telling you this as a professional signalsman, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I just might say something, page 77, lines 24 and 25, the witness said: There are no elements for work according to this document, whereas the transcript does not reflect that literally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No date, no other elements. Okay. Based on everything else that we can see there, can you perhaps determine what year we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be 1998 because of Ibar IK, what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness. If I just may have an opportunity to wish everyone a merry Christmas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before we show our next witness in, I would seek permission to address you. Last Thursday we received witness notification and last Monday we realized that there might be more time left that there might be some idle run on our part, and we additionally called this witness, Goran Mijatovic [as interpreted] I proofed him yesterday and all we have is 45 minutes. It will be impossible for me to complete my examination-in-chief. He will have to return both for the end of my chief and for the cross. It was late in the day yesterday, but I realized that there was the option of doing a 92 ter statement, and then maybe we could handle some details for between 20 and 30 minutes, I mean live with this witness. It was too late in the day yesterday to inform the OTP, we could have drawn up the statement but we couldn't have kept it within the Rules. The witness would have to remain under oath for a full month. I think both for my Defence and for the Court, it might make sense. I realize that we would even save up some time, even if you take these 45 minutes away and then one and a half hours -- and then up to two hours, and that is the time I envisaged for my chief, just not to keep him under oath for a full month and not to start now. So what I propose is, if you agree, that he be the first witness to appear after the break and to make him a 92 ter witness plus appearing live, but not for more than half an hour. I thought there might be more -- I apologise, just to say this again. I thought there might be more time left for us today, and just to avoid wasting time I called this witness. However, in view of how much time remains, I would ask the Trial Chamber to review my proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Obviously this is a matter for the Court, but we have no objections except for an observation. Firstly, we were told about the witness Goran Jeftovic so if the Defence were thinking about calling Goran Mijatovic, we would object to him being called if that was our intention because we were told about Jeftovic. Secondly, the proposal of learned counsel would, in fact, save significant time if he does proceed by way of 92 ter. Those are the observations we would make.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's an interpretation error, no more than that. My learned friend Stamp is quite right, the transcript reads "Mijatovic," what I actually said was "Jeftovic," Goran Jeftovic, as opposed to Goran Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The suggestion you make, Mr. Bakrac, only has force because of the situation you yourself have effectively created. You are the man that told us your case would finish today, and therefore it comes as quite astounding that we should get to this stage in the day and you effectively tell us that you're not in a position to proceed economically and reasonably with the next witness. And the reason I mention this is to emphasise what we said yesterday, that all the signs are so far that you haven't really applied your mind adequately to how to introduce all the evidence you wish to introduce within the time constraints that we all must work under. I hope that the next few weeks will see a change in that approach, and that by giving you another 45 minutes to sort out your problems we may see spectacular results. So in the true spirit of the colour of the robes that we wear, we will grant your motion, and it's the closest you'll ever get to a Christmas greeting from this Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a special Christmas assignment, but at any rate I can only thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will therefore adjourn now, and we will resume, I'm told, in court III -- sorry, before I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, there's one procedural matter we wanted to raise before the end of the year, IC0163 and P3048 were maps that were discussed in private session yesterday with Witness SD-1. We neglected to mention that we wanted to tender those under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the status of these documents will be changed. They will now be under seal. So we'll adjourn and resume on Wednesday, the 16th of January, at 2.15, in court III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I also wish to wish you all a happy Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of January, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.07 p.m.,
